name: Jonathan Hager House

location.text: 110 Key Street, Hagerstown City Park, Washington County, Maryland

dates.altered: Sold with increased acreage to Jacob Rohrer in 1745 and held by the Rohrers and their descendants the Hammonds until 1944; acquired by the Washington County Historical Society, given to the City of Hagerstown in 1954 and opened as a museum in 1962. 'Restored; building largely original' (survey). The roof is now covered with Williamsburg-type tiles imitating the wooden shingles the house appears once to have had, and a concrete floor and flagstones were added to the cellar in restoration, raising it about eight inches.
dates.note: The survey says 'Date of Erection: Circa 1740' and reasons that Hager built it between June 1739 and 1745, probably about the time of his marriage in 1740. The city and the Washington County Historical Trust both say 1739. Hager bought the 200-acre tract 'Hager's Fancy' from Daniel Dulany on 5 June 1739, and an October 1739 survey of the property already refers to 'Hager's dwelling house'.

quotes.text: THE JONATHAN HAGSR HOUSE Hagerstown, Washington County, Maryland. Owner: The Washington County Historical Society, Hagerstown, Maryland. Date of Erection: Circa 1740. Architect: Unknown. Builder: Jonathan Hager, founder of Hagerstown, Maryland. Present Condition: Restored; building largely original. Number of Stories: Two and one-half above cellar, which is banked on one side.

Materials of Construction: . Exterior walls - small fieldstones removed from the surrounding natural limestone out-cropping. Interior walls - mud-and-rye-straw plaster over 1 by 4 inch oak strips laid horizontally an approximate 2 inches apart.

Chimney - brick, capped, and emerging in a near-central position in the roof-line. Originates in a limestone hearth and flue on the ground-floor level. Roof - now covered with Williamsburg-type tiles, in imitation of the wooden shingles which the house appears to have once had. Floors - ground floor, flagstone; remainder of floors largely early replacements in pine, oak and walnut random- width boards.

The bottom floor consists of three rooms, in two of which are springs which join. In the south room there is an enormous fireplace. Neither of the other rooms has a fireplace, and it seems unlikely that they were used for anything but storage.

measurements.note: Two of the three contain the springs; one has an enormous fireplace and served as the principal kitchen. The other two the surveyor thinks were storage only.

note: The bank house stated by a federal surveyor in one line -- 'Two and one-half above cellar, which is banked on one side' -- and the only such statement this cluster found. It also contains an argument the corpus should read before it repeats the fortification story: the surveyor explicitly REFUSES the defensive reading of the spring and of the splayed openings ('It is therefore not neces-sary to assume that the house was built over a spring with an eye ... to withstanding a siege from Indians'), and grounds the spring in dairy, laundry and cold storage instead -- three sentences before allowing that the house 'may likewise be regarded as a house-fort'. The node's own prose reaches the same conclusion by the same route: it is a refrigerator obtained for the cost of moving earth.
